result:
I want to write about a metal cylinder in a vault outside Paris, because I think it had one of the strangest jobs ever given to an object.

From 1889 to 2019, the kilogram was a physical thing: a cylinder of platinum and iridium, a little smaller than a golf ball, kept under three nested bell jars in Sèvres. Opening its vault took three keys held by three different people. Everything else in the world that weighed a kilogram did so by matching it, through a long chain of copies of copies.

This meant the cylinder could not be wrong. A fingerprint on it would, strictly speaking, have made everything else in the universe slightly lighter. Wittgenstein made a similar point about the standard meter bar, which lived nearby: it is the one object of which you can say neither that it is a meter long nor that it isn't. A ruler can't measure itself.

The trouble is that the cylinder was also just a lump of metal, and lumps of metal change. Every few decades it was taken out and compared with its official copies, and over a century they drifted apart by about 50 micrograms, roughly the mass of an eyelash. Nobody could say which had changed. The measurements showed only a difference, and the definition insisted that the prototype was the one thing that had stayed put. Metrologists knew that was probably false, and they had no way to express how false.

So in 2019 they retired it. The kilogram is now defined by fixing the value of the Planck constant, and a device called a Kibble balance can produce one by weighing mass against electromagnetic force. Any well-equipped lab can now make a kilogram from scratch without asking France. That was the ambition of the metric system from the 1790s, when its founders dedicated it "to all times, to all peoples" and then, lacking anything better, had to settle for a bar and a weight in a cabinet.

I'm drawn to this story because it shows how something that feels abstract and permanent, like a unit, can rest on something small and fragile. For 130 years, the precision of every pharmacy scale and physics experiment traced back to one object that people were afraid to touch.

My favorite part is that the cylinder is still there, in the same vault, under the same jars. People still measure it, but now they do it to find out how much it weighs. For most of its life that question had no meaning, and today the answer is one kilogram, give or take a few micrograms.
